topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Carefully integrating complementary behavioral priors from multiple specialized agents via a novel **Alignment-Based Behavioral Fusion (ABBF)** architecture reduces policy interference and negative transfer, enabling improved zero-shot generalization on diverse, out-of-distribution tasks by explicitly aligning and preserving non-conflicting strategies in a unified latent space.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains a major challenge, especially when deploying agents trained on limited task distributions to unseen environments. Naive policy fusion or single-agent training often suffers from negative transfer and catastrophic forgetting due to conflicting strategies embedded in learned policies. Existing multi-task and meta-learning methods lack explicit mechanisms to align and disentangle behavioral priors, limiting compositional generalization across diverse tasks.

APPROACH:  
We propose **ABBF**, a multi-task/meta-learning architecture that explicitly aligns latent representations of pre-trained behavioral priors from disjoint task subsets to preserve complementary strategies and mitigate destructive interference. Alignment and disentanglement are quantitatively operationalized via metrics such as cosine similarity of latent embeddings, negative transfer ratios, and forgetting curves. The architecture incorporates specialized modules (e.g., attention-based fusion layers and orthogonality constraints) designed to maintain modularity of behaviors, allowing recombination rather than averaging or overwriting. An ablation baseline performs naive policy averaging or concatenation without alignment, isolating the causal effect of ABBF’s alignment mechanism.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on Meta-World ML45 and ML10 manipulation task suites, training behavioral priors on disjoint subsets of tasks to ensure complementarity. Zero-shot success rate on held-out, out-of-distribution tasks—with varying object properties and goals—serves as the primary metric. Baselines include (a) single-agent training from scratch, (b) naive fusion via averaging/concatenation, (c) ensemble voting, and (d) capacity- and data-matched models without alignment. Statistical tests (e.g., paired t-tests, p < 0.05) assess significance of >10% absolute improvement by ABBF. Diagnostic analyses verify that ABBF reduces interference and preserves complementary behaviors, confirming the proposed causal mechanism. Failure modes include parity or superiority of naive fusion, which would falsify the hypothesis and direct follow-up studies increasing capacity without alignment.

NOVELTY:  
ABBF explicitly formalizes and operationalizes behavioral prior alignment as a requisite for effective fusion, advancing beyond prior modular or meta-RL approaches that lack interference-mitigating mechanisms. By combining theoretical insights from representation learning and transfer theory with concrete quantitative diagnostics, this work uniquely links alignment-induced disentanglement to zero-shot compositional generalization in reinforcement learning.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Training reinforcement learning policies with *Balanced Adversarial Perturbation Robustness*—simultaneous, physically plausible adversarial modifications to both transition dynamics and observation noise—disentangles robustness to environment stochasticity from sensory noise, thereby improving zero-shot generalization to unseen environment variations.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in RL remains a significant challenge because policies often overfit to either the dynamics or observation characteristics of the training environment, limiting transfer to new domains. While domain randomization and robust RL methods address variation in either observations or dynamics, they rarely enforce robustness jointly, risking vulnerabilities to unmodeled perturbations. A principled approach that explicitly disentangles these robustness aspects is needed to ensure reliable deployment in diverse, realistic environments.

APPROACH:  
We propose training policies under *Balanced Adversarial Perturbation Robustness* (BAPR), where adversarial perturbations to transition dynamics (e.g., joint friction, mass) and observation noise (e.g., sensor calibration errors) are jointly optimized within physically plausible constraints. This incentivizes the policy to learn invariant representations and control strategies robust to both environment evolution and sensory corruption, grounded in Invariant Risk Minimization and domain randomization theory. We include ablations training with perturbations only on observations or only on dynamics to isolate the causal mechanism.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate policies trained under BAPR, observation-only, and dynamics-only adversarial perturbations on MuJoCo continuous control tasks (Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah) using standardized zero-shot benchmarks from the RELLIS robustness gym and D4RL perturbed variants. Metrics include normalized cumulative reward across zero-shot test environments exhibiting unseen observation noise, dynamics shifts, or both; sensitivity analyses; and disentanglement scores on learned representations. Statistical significance will be assessed via paired t-tests comparing BAPR to baselines including domain randomization (Peng et al., 2018) and abstract representation methods (2025).

NOVELTY:  
This work formalizes and empirically validates the *Balanced Adversarial Perturbation Robustness* mechanism as a causal driver of zero-shot generalization, explicitly disentangling robustness to transition dynamics and observation noise—going beyond prior domain randomization or single-domain robustness approaches by leveraging joint, physically constrained adversarial training. This principled disentanglement and the associated experimental regime uniquely clarify the distinct and complementary contributions of dynamics and observation invariance to policy transfer performance.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Incorporating explicitly structured and verified causal graphs into reinforcement learning policies enhances zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution environments by leveraging invariant causal mechanisms rather than spurious correlations.

BACKGROUND: Reinforcement learning agents often fail to generalize zero-shot to environments with unseen dynamics due to overfitting to correlational or superficial patterns in training data. While data augmentation and contrastive representation learning partially address this, they lack principled grounding in the underlying environment structure. Exploiting the causal invariance principle—where causal mechanisms remain stable under interventions—offers a promising pathway to robust, transferable policies.

APPROACH: We propose training RL agents augmented with explicitly defined structured causal models encoding environment latent variables, causal edges, and functional dependencies, obtained via available ground-truth graphs or learned through constrained causal discovery methods. This causal-graph-augmented agent will be compared against (1) an ablation variant using randomized/scrambled causal graphs to isolate the effect of correct causal knowledge, and (2) standard model-free baselines such as Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The agents use the causal graph for either model-based planning or causally informed representation learning, explicitly leveraging invariant causal relationships to adapt to unseen environment dynamics.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluation occurs on the CausalWorld benchmark with known robotic manipulation causal graphs and the Procgen benchmark where environment parameters systematically shift, testing zero-shot generalization by training on subsets of dynamics and evaluating on disjoint, out-of-distribution scenarios. Metrics include average episodic return and success rate, with statistically significant improvements assessed over at least 10 random seeds using confidence intervals and hypothesis testing, where a ≥10% gain over baselines indicates meaningful generalization benefit.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work relying on implicit or learned latent factors without causal constraints, this approach explicitly integrates well-defined causal graphs into RL policy architecture and rigorously controls for architectural complexity via scrambled-graph ablations. It critically evaluates the causal invariance assumption’s practical utility in zero-shot generalization and carefully addresses causal graph acquisition challenges, thus bridging causal inference theory with scalable RL generalization beyond existing augmentation or contrastive methods.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Reinforcement learning agents that explicitly learn task-agnostic, causally disentangled state representations via invariant causal mechanism discovery will demonstrate significantly improved zero-shot generalization to unseen environments compared to agents using contrastive or augmentation-only representations.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains a critical challenge because learned policies often exploit spurious correlations in training environments, leading to brittle performance under distributional shifts. While contrastive and augmentation-based approaches enforce superficial invariances, they do not guarantee factorization along stable causal generative factors, limiting transfer to novel domains with altered spurious features.

APPROACH: We propose integrating an invariant causal representation learning objective into the RL agent’s state encoder, leveraging principles from Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) adapted for model-free RL, to discover latent factors whose effect on rewards and transitions remains stable across diverse training environments. This causal disentanglement is operationalized by jointly optimizing policy and encoder under multiple environment interventions created via domain randomization, without relying on ground-truth causal graphs. A matched architecture ablation with a standard variational autoencoder (VAE) objective controls for model capacity, isolating the causal mechanism’s effect.

EXPERIMENT: We train three groups of RL agents—(1) causal disentanglement (IRM-based), (2) contrastive baseline (CURL), and (3) ablation (VAE without causal constraints)—on the Procgen benchmark and Distracting Control Suite, carefully matching architectures and training budgets. Zero-shot generalization is evaluated by normalized average episode return on held-out procedurally generated levels and visual/dynamics shifts, with statistical significance assessed over 10 seeds and multiple environment instances. A targeted causal factor intervention test masks learned latent factors at test time to verify causal mechanism load-bearing by measuring performance degradation exclusive to the causal group.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior approaches that enforce invariance through data augmentations or contrastive losses, our method explicitly discovers stable causal mechanisms underlying state dynamics and rewards without supervisory causal knowledge, enabling principled disentanglement that generalizes robustly across environment domains. This rigorously validated causal disentanglement objective, combined with a falsification intervention, distinguishes our contribution by directly linking causal factorization to zero-shot policy generalization.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Training reinforcement learning agents with hierarchical multi-level environment dynamics randomization combined with explicit disentangled representation learning of invariant causal factors improves zero-shot generalization beyond single-level randomization or mere exposure to variability.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization remains a critical challenge in reinforcement learning, where policies trained in limited environments fail to transfer robustly to unseen conditions. Prior domain randomization methods typically vary a single aspect of environment dynamics (e.g., physics or sensory noise), which risks overfitting to unvaried features and limits generalization. Addressing this requires principled mechanisms to learn representations that abstract away spurious correlations and capture invariant causal factors across multiple hierarchical levels of environment variation.

APPROACH:  
We propose a framework combining controlled multi-level environment randomization—simultaneously varying physics parameters (mass, friction), task goals (goal positions, target velocities), and sensory noise (observation corruption, sensor dropout)—with explicit disentangled representation learning modules (e.g., variational or contrastive factorization architectures) designed to isolate independent causal factors across these levels. This approach operationalizes the causal mechanism of *invariance learning* and *causal abstraction* (Schölkopf et al., 2021), compelling the agent to extract invariant features that causally govern task dynamics, thereby enabling robust zero-shot transfer.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on MuJoCo locomotion tasks (Hopper, Walker2d, Ant) and Meta-World MT10 benchmark, training agents under: (i) physics-only randomization, (ii) task-goal-only randomization, (iii) sensory noise-only randomization, (iv) combined multi-level randomization with disentangled representation learning, and (v) an ablation variant with multi-level randomization but disabled disentanglement modules. Zero-shot generalization is measured as normalized episodic return averaged over 50 held-out environments featuring novel friction-mass-goal-noise combinations unseen during training. Baselines include PPO, SAC without randomization, and prior single-level randomization methods (Pinto et al., 2017; Rajeswaran et al., 2017). A ≥15% absolute improvement over best single-level baselines and significant performance drop in the ablation would confirm the hypothesized causal mechanism.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly formalizes and tests the causal role of disentangled invariant representation learning under hierarchical multi-level environment randomization, moving beyond prior domain randomization efforts that focus on single-level variability or treat representation learning implicitly. The integration of causal abstraction principles with controlled environment variability and mechanism-driven ablations uniquely advances theoretical and empirical understanding of zero-shot generalization in RL.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating feature-space density estimation via expressive normalizing flows into deep neural network uncertainty quantification pipelines explicitly models representation likelihoods, thereby reducing overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs more effectively than ensemble or Bayesian methods alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Current uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods in deep neural networks—such as Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), Monte Carlo Dropout, and ensembles—primarily capture predictive uncertainty without explicitly modeling the probability distribution of learned feature representations. This absence limits their ability to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and often results in overconfident misclassifications. Leveraging feature-space density estimation addresses this gap by identifying low-density regions where uncertainty should naturally increase, a principle supported by density-ratio estimation theory (Sugiyama et al., 2012).

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting a standard deep neural network classifier with a normalizing flow module trained on the penultimate layer’s feature embeddings to estimate their density distribution. The final uncertainty estimate combines predictive uncertainty (from either a Bayesian or ensemble classifier) with the feature-space likelihood score from the normalizing flow via a calibrated fusion strategy. Ablations include replacing the flow with a simple Gaussian density model and evaluating predictive uncertainty alone, to isolate the causal contribution of expressive density estimation.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will train models on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and evaluate OOD detection performance on SVHN and TinyImageNet respectively, measuring AUROC for OOD detection, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on in-distribution data, and Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) baselines. Multiple random seeds and data splits will ensure robustness, and we will report computational cost and training stability. Success requires at least a 5 percentage point AUROC improvement over ensembles and BNN/MC Dropout baselines plus fewer than 1% of OOD samples with over 90% confidence. Failure or parity with Gaussian density ablations will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that focuses solely on predictive uncertainty or uses simple density models, our method explicitly integrates expressive normalizing flows to capture complex feature distributions, with a rigorously designed causal isolation via ablations and fusion strategies. We also provide theoretical grounding addressing known limitations of likelihood-based OOD detection and establish principled uncertainty combination, thereby advancing beyond existing UQ techniques and demonstrating practical, calibrated improvements in OOD robustness.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Utilize contrastive representation learning to embed uncertainty estimates such that the geometric structure of the learned latent space causally improves uncertainty calibration under domain shift compared to traditional Bayesian neural network methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) in deep neural networks remains challenging, especially under domain shifts where models face distributional changes unseen during training. Traditional Bayesian methods estimate uncertainty via weight posterior approximations but often lack adaptability to shifts because the learned representations are not explicitly structured to reflect semantic similarity or uncertainty geometry. This limits their calibration and robustness in real-world applications requiring trustworthy predictions.

APPROACH:  
We propose a contrastive uncertainty embedding mechanism where a contrastive loss explicitly structures the representation space so that semantically similar inputs cluster tightly and dissimilar inputs are separated, encoding uncertainty as a function of geometric properties such as embedding density or distance. An uncertainty estimation head is trained uniformly across methods to predict calibrated uncertainty scores from these embeddings. We isolate the causal role of the contrastive loss by ablating it while keeping all other components identical, and further test its complementarity by combining Bayesian uncertainty estimation on top of the contrastive embeddings.

EXPERIMENT:  
We benchmark on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C to evaluate uncertainty calibration under synthetic corruptions, and on DomainNet by training on the Real domain and testing on Sketch and Painting domains to assess real-world domain shifts. Baselines include Bayesian Neural Networks (Bayes by Backprop) and Monte Carlo Dropout applied to identical ResNet-50 architectures with a fixed uncertainty estimation head. Metrics include Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), and Brier score measured on both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets. Success requires a ≥20% reduction in ECE compared to baselines under domain shifts without degradation in NLL, and failure if the contrastive loss ablation matches contrastive performance or all models degrade similarly.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that primarily applies Bayesian or ensemble uncertainty on fixed representations, our method explicitly leverages contrastive learning as a causal intervention shaping embedding geometry to encode uncertainty, a relational inductive bias overlooked in classical Bayesian formulations. We provide a rigorous empirical and theoretical framework to isolate and validate this mechanism under controlled domain shifts, differentiating embedding structure effects from mere accuracy or capacity improvements.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Utilizing uncertainty-calibrated, feature-space adversarial perturbations guided by Bayesian uncertainty estimates enhances out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in deep neural networks beyond standard Monte Carlo dropout and uncalibrated adversarial approaches.

BACKGROUND:  
Reliable OOD detection remains a critical challenge in deploying deep neural networks in safety-sensitive applications, where models must recognize inputs that differ from training distributions. Existing uncertainty quantification methods like Bayesian dropout provide passive uncertainty estimates but often fail to sufficiently discriminate OOD samples. Moreover, adversarial perturbations have been used to probe model vulnerabilities, but their integration with calibrated uncertainty to actively amplify OOD signals is underexplored.

APPROACH:  
We propose a method that generates adversarial perturbations in selected deep feature layers—specifically, mid-to-high level convolutional activations—using projected gradient descent (PGD) constrained by an ℓ₂-norm ball calibrated via Bayesian dropout uncertainty gradients. This uncertainty calibration explicitly optimizes perturbations toward regions of maximal predictive entropy or mutual information, ensuring perturbed features remain within the valid manifold via a learned feature-to-input decoder for validity verification. The method includes rigorous uncertainty calibration validation using expected calibration error (ECE) and reliability diagrams before perturbation.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate OOD detection performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution datasets, with SVHN and TinyImageNet as OOD benchmarks, comparing AUROC and FPR95 metrics across three key conditions: (1) baseline MC-dropout uncertainty without perturbation, (2) feature-space PGD adversarial perturbations without uncertainty guidance, and (3) full uncertainty-calibrated feature-space adversarial perturbations. Additional baselines include input-space adversarial perturbations, deep ensembles, Mahalanobis distance detection, and ODIN, with controlled model capacities and identical training protocols. The hypothesis is falsified if the full method fails to improve AUROC by ≥5% and reduce FPR95 by ≥10% over both the MC-dropout baseline and uncalibrated perturbations.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates uncertainty calibration gradients into the generation of feature-space adversarial perturbations, explicitly leveraging model uncertainty geometry to amplify OOD signals—a causal mechanism not addressed by existing adversarial or uncertainty quantification methods. It advances beyond prior work by coupling calibrated uncertainty-driven feature perturbations with validation of perturbation validity and comprehensive ablations, thus providing a theoretically grounded and empirically rigorous framework for OOD detection enhancement.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating input-gradient-based sensitivity measures into the Bayesian inference framework of neural networks—via a principled gradient-sensitivity regularization term in the variational objective—significantly improves uncertainty calibration under distributional shifts compared to standard Bayesian neural networks.

BACKGROUND: Reliable uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks remains challenging, especially under distributional shift and corrupted inputs, because standard Bayesian methods typically model uncertainty only over parameters, ignoring input feature relevance and sensitivity. This oversight limits the model’s ability to capture epistemic uncertainty arising from variations in input features that causally influence predictions, reducing calibration quality and robustness in high-stakes applications.

APPROACH: We formalize a causal mechanism named *Gradient-Sensitivity Bayesian Inference* that integrates input-gradient magnitudes—measuring local feature sensitivity—directly into the variational Bayesian objective as an auxiliary likelihood-inspired term, preserving a probabilistic interpretation and principled uncertainty quantification. The approach trains a Sensitivity-BNN by jointly optimizing the standard Bayesian posterior approximation and a gradient-sensitivity regularizer weighted to enforce alignment between prediction uncertainty and input feature influence, thereby capturing epistemic uncertainty due to both model parameters and input perturbations.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate Sensitivity-BNN versus standard Bayesian baselines—MC Dropout, Bayes by Backprop, and deep ensembles—using CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution datasets, CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C for corrupted data, and TinyImageNet and SVHN as out-of-distribution test sets. Metrics include Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), and outlier detection AUC-ROC based on uncertainty scores. Ablation studies will compare Sensitivity-BNN against identical BNN architectures without gradient regularization and against controls such as random gradient masking and generic input-dependent regularizers. Statistical power analysis will ensure significance of observed improvements.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior UQ methods that focus solely on parameter uncertainty or heuristically incorporate sensitivity, this work explicitly and rigorously integrates input-gradient-based causal sensitivity into Bayesian inference with a mathematically justified auxiliary term, enabling principled joint modeling of parameter and input-derived epistemic uncertainty. This establishes a novel theoretical and empirical link between model interpretability (causal feature attribution) and uncertainty calibration, advancing robustness to distributional shifts beyond existing Bayesian techniques.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating a late-stage uncertainty-focused attention mechanism—termed **Uncertainty Signal Amplification (USA)**—within deep ensemble architectures selectively enhances uncertainty-relevant latent features, thereby disentangling and improving the localization and interpretability of predictive uncertainty compared to conventional feed-forward or generic attention models.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate and interpretable uncertainty quantification (UQ) in deep neural networks remains a critical challenge for high-stakes applications such as medical imaging, where precise spatial localization of uncertain predictions can guide clinical decision-making. Conventional ensemble methods effectively capture holistic epistemic uncertainty but often produce diffuse or entangled uncertainty maps lacking clear interpretability. Existing attention mechanisms are typically generic and not explicitly optimized to highlight uncertainty signals, limiting their utility in refining uncertainty localization.

APPROACH:  
We propose the **Uncertainty Signal Amplification (USA)** mechanism, an architectural module applied at the output stage of each ensemble member that is explicitly trained to attend to latent features statistically correlated with uncertainty estimates (e.g., output variance from MC dropout runs or ensemble disagreement). This selective attention re-weights uncertainty-relevant features, thereby disentangling predictive uncertainty from confounding feature noise. When combined with deep ensembles, USA enables clearer and more interpretable uncertainty localization. The approach includes control experiments with generic attention modules, attention with randomized weights, and attention applied at varying network depths to isolate the causal role of USA.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate three model variants—(1) feed-forward deep ensembles without attention, (2) ensembles with generic attention modules, and (3) ensembles with the USA module—on the NIH Chest X-ray14 and LIDC-IDRI datasets, leveraging expert-annotated uncertainty regions and multi-label disease classification tasks. Metrics include Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for calibration, Uncertainty Localization Accuracy (ULA) measured by overlap (IoU/Dice) between high-uncertainty regions and expert-annotated ambiguous areas or misclassifications, and Mutual Information Gap (MIG) quantifying alignment between attention weights and uncertainty maps. Ablation studies with randomized and multi-layer attention will ensure robustness. A significant improvement of at least 10% in ULA and reductions in ECE for (3) over (1) and (2) will support the hypothesis; failure to do so would falsify the causal mechanism.

NOVELTY:  
This work introduces the USA mechanism that explicitly exploits uncertainty-correlated latent features via attention at a late network stage, a novel approach beyond standard ensemble or generic attention methods. By explicitly disentangling uncertainty signals within the representation, it bridges the gap between holistic epistemic uncertainty estimation and spatial uncertainty interpretability—a critical advancement not addressed by prior UQ techniques or attention-based models in deep learning.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Agents endowed with heterogeneous, biologically plausible sensory modalities develop emergent communication protocols that are more efficient and robust under noisy communication channels than agents with homogeneous modalities, with modality diversity causally necessary for these improvements as shown by controlled ablation of sensory input diversity.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in multi-agent systems often assumes homogeneous sensory inputs, limiting robustness when communication channels are noisy. Biological multisensory integration demonstrates that redundancy and complementary modalities reduce uncertainty and enhance information transmission. However, the causal role of sensory modality diversity in fostering robust emergent communication protocols under noise remains an open problem in artificial multi-agent learning.

APPROACH:  
We simulate agents with distinct, physically plausible sensory modalities (vision, tactile, auditory) within an extended MultiAgent Particle Environment featuring custom noisy communication channels. Two primary groups are trained: (1) heterogeneous modality agents with non-overlapping, modality-specific sensory inputs, and (2) homogeneous modality agents receiving identical sensory data. A rigorous ablation baseline is introduced by training agents with heterogeneous sensory inputs but restricting communication to a single shared modality channel during testing, isolating the effect of modality diversity in communication.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate all groups on a cooperative navigation and object manipulation task under varying controlled noise levels introduced via a parametrized Gaussian channel model. Metrics include task completion rate, communication efficiency (bits per successful communication episode measured on encoded messages post-processing), and robustness quantified by performance degradation as noise increases. Baselines include the homogeneous agents, ablated heterogeneous communication condition, and an oracle noiseless communication upper bound.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely operationalizes biologically inspired, modality-specific sensory inputs within emergent communication benchmarks and introduces a causal ablation that disentangles sensory input diversity from communication channel configurations. It offers a formalized experimental protocol quantifying modality diversity’s necessity for robust emergent communication, advancing beyond prior correlational findings and integrating multisensory information theory principles with multi-agent reinforcement learning.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Introducing the **Bandwidth-Heterogeneity-Task Interaction Mechanism**, whereby asymmetric communication bandwidth constraints combined with agent heterogeneity and task-dependent environmental demands induce emergent hierarchical communication roles in multi-agent systems, while uniform communication patterns arise when robustness or redundancy are prioritized.

BACKGROUND: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems frequently rely on communication protocols to coordinate complex cooperative behaviors; however, the origins of hierarchical communication structures remain poorly understood. Existing work often overlooks how the interplay of communication constraints, agent diversity, and environmental task asymmetries drives role specialization and hierarchical organization, limiting insights into the causal factors that shape emergent communication topologies.

APPROACH: We propose a fully factorial MARL experimental framework manipulating three factors independently and in combination—communication bandwidth asymmetry, agent heterogeneity (e.g., differing unit classes), and task/environment asymmetry (e.g., spatial or temporal information gradients)—to isolate their causal effects on communication role emergence. Communication graphs derived from learned protocols will be analyzed using rigorous statistical hierarchy metrics (degree centralization, betweenness centrality variance), complemented by robustness and redundancy measures and qualitative role-function verification, ensuring reproducible and interpretable findings.

EXPERIMENT: Using the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) dataset, agents will be trained under systematically varied bandwidth constraints and environmental/task heterogeneity, with ablation baselines including symmetric bandwidth with/without heterogeneity and task asymmetry, and uniform bandwidth multi-agent communication baselines (e.g., CommNet, TarMAC). Success metrics include statistically significant emergence of hierarchical communication topologies (degree centralization > 0.3 and elevated betweenness centrality variance beyond random graphs), improved cooperative task performance (win rates), and communication robustness indices.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly formalizes and empirically validates the **Bandwidth-Heterogeneity-Task Interaction Mechanism**, advancing beyond prior studies that consider communication constraints or agent heterogeneity in isolation by leveraging a factorial design that rigorously disentangles their combined causal influence on emergent communication hierarchies. It further bridges organizational theory and network science with MARL, providing transparent, multimodal hierarchy detection protocols and operationalizing bandwidth constraints within end-to-end learning, thereby offering novel theoretical and methodological insights into the formation of communication roles in complex multi-agent systems.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems endowed with heterogeneous, complementary sensory modalities develop more efficient and functionally informative emergent communication protocols than systems with homogeneous sensory inputs under matched task constraints, driven by the causal mechanism of *complementary information integration*.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in multi-agent systems often assumes homogeneous sensory inputs, limiting the diversity of information agents must share. However, many real-world cooperative tasks involve agents with distinct, non-redundant perception streams, raising the question of whether sensor heterogeneity inherently promotes richer and more efficient communication protocols. Addressing this gap is critical for advancing scalable, adaptive multi-agent coordination beyond existing paradigms focused on partial observability or role differentiation alone.

APPROACH:  
We operationalize the causal mechanism of complementary information integration by constructing multi-agent systems in a controlled cooperative navigation and object identification environment (e.g., extended Multi-Agent Particle Environment with multimodal inputs) with two key experimental conditions: (1) heterogeneous sensory modalities assigned uniquely per agent (vision, sonar, tactile), and (2) homogeneous sensory modalities identical across all agents. A sensor homogenization ablation baseline—artificially averaging or masking heterogeneous sensory data—disrupts complementary information, explicitly testing causality. Communication efficiency is quantified using bias-corrected normalized mutual information (NMI) between discrete, task-relevant state encodings and messages, alongside communication bandwidth (bits per timestep) and task success rates.

EXPERIMENT:  
Agents are trained with matched architectures, hyperparameters, and random seeds across three conditions (heterogeneous, homogeneous, and ablation). Success metrics include a ≥20% increase in NMI and ≥10% increase in task success at equal or lower communication bandwidth for heterogeneous versus homogeneous agents, and a ≥15% performance drop in the ablation baseline compared to intact heterogeneity. Robustness is verified by multiple environment variations and statistical significance testing.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focusing on emergent communication under partial observability or compositionality without explicit sensor diversity (e.g., Foerster et al., 2016; Lazaridou et al., 2018), this study rigorously tests the *causal role* of sensor heterogeneity in driving communication efficiency through complementary information integration. The inclusion of a sensor homogenization ablation uniquely isolates sensory diversity as the mechanistic driver, advancing theoretical and practical understanding of when and why emergent protocols become more efficient in multi-agent systems.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems that integrate heterogeneous sensory modalities via explicit multisensory Bayesian fusion mechanisms develop more efficient and robust emergent communication protocols under noisy conditions compared to homogeneous or ablated multisensory systems.

BACKGROUND:  
Current emergent communication research largely focuses on homogeneous sensory inputs or purely learned integration without explicitly modeling multisensory fusion principles. However, real-world communication benefits from multisensory integration, which reduces uncertainty by combining complementary sensory cues. The causal role of multisensory integration mechanisms in enhancing communication robustness and efficiency in noisy multi-agent environments remains an open problem.

APPROACH:  
We propose equipping multi-agent systems with heterogeneous sensory modalities (e.g., vision and audition) combined through a differentiable Bayesian fusion layer that enforces theoretically grounded multisensory integration. This inductive bias explicitly models complementary and redundant information fusion, enabling principled error correction and uncertainty reduction. We compare these agents to homogeneous sensory agents and to heterogeneous sensory agents with ablated fusion layers that disable multisensory integration while keeping architecture and training protocols constant.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using an extended Multi-Agent Particle Environment augmented with noise injection protocols derived from the Audio-Visual Event (AVE) dataset, agents perform cooperative communication tasks under graded modality-specific noise levels. Metrics include communication efficiency (bits per successful message), robustness (success rate across increasing noise), and compositionality (topographical similarity scores per Andreas, 2019). Baselines include homogeneous sensory agents trained with and without noise and standard emergent communication architectures adapted from the SCAN dataset.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly integrates and tests a theoretically principled multisensory Bayesian fusion mechanism within emergent communication protocols, rigorously isolating the causal effect of multisensory integration on robustness and efficiency. Unlike prior approaches relying solely on heterogeneous inputs or learned fusion, our method enforces fusion inductive biases and employs a novel ablation design that preserves training dynamics, providing a clear mechanistic understanding of multisensory contributions in multi-agent communication under noise.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Dynamically reconfigurable communication topologies enable multi-agent systems to develop more efficient and compositional emergent languages than fixed-topology systems by adaptively optimizing information pathways in task-relevant interactions.

BACKGROUND: Efficient emergent communication in multi-agent systems remains a key challenge, particularly under constraints of compositional language demands and environmental complexity. Existing work often assumes fixed communication topologies, limiting adaptive information flow and possibly hindering language efficiency and compositionality, a gap that adaptive network reconfiguration may address.

APPROACH: We investigate the causal role of **adaptive network reconfiguration**—a process where agents selectively update communication links based on interaction success and utility feedback—to optimize communication pathways dynamically. This is contrasted against fixed topology networks and random topology rewiring baselines, with a mechanism ablation condition isolating dynamic reconfiguration effects from static structural differences.

EXPERIMENT: Agents are trained on referential games using the SCAN dataset, controlling for environment and agent capabilities. We measure emergent communication efficiency via communication bandwidth (bits per successful task), compositionality using normalized topographic similarity metrics, and task accuracy. Statistical comparison across dynamic, fixed, random-rewiring, and ablation conditions tests if dynamic topology reconfiguration yields significantly higher efficiency and compositionality without sacrificing accuracy.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely operationalizes and rigorously controls for adaptive topology changes in emergent communication, explicitly linking network science principles of adaptive reconfiguration to language efficiency. Unlike prior studies that focus solely on fixed or random topologies or impose architectural biases, our design isolates the causal mechanism of topology flexibility under compositional language demands, advancing understanding of network-structured communication emergence.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrating AlphaFold-predicted static structures as anchored starting points for enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics simulations will causally improve the accuracy of predicted protein conformational ensembles under physiological conditions, as validated quantitatively against multi-timescale NMR relaxation observables.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold produces highly accurate static protein structures representing low-energy conformations but does not explicitly capture conformational heterogeneity or dynamics critical for protein function under physiological conditions. Existing MD simulations can sample dynamics but often suffer from inadequate sampling or lack experimentally grounded initial states, limiting their predictive accuracy for dynamic ensembles. Bridging static structural predictions with dynamic ensemble modeling remains an open challenge for accurately describing protein motions relevant to biology.

APPROACH: Starting from AlphaFold-generated static models, we will perform all-atom MD simulations augmented with advanced enhanced sampling methods (e.g., replica exchange, metadynamics) to extensively explore conformational space. We will standardize force fields and solvent conditions and apply validated, reproducible computational pipelines to derive NMR relaxation parameters (Lipari-Szabo order parameters S², Rex rates) from simulation trajectories. Comparative arms include unbiased MD from AlphaFold starts, enhanced sampling MD from homology or random coil models, and static AlphaFold structures alone, enabling explicit causal testing of the AlphaFold initialization mechanism.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark predicted dynamic ensembles against high-quality multi-timescale NMR relaxation datasets from BMRB entries such as ubiquitin (BMRB 6457), GB3 domain (BMRB 15156), and calmodulin (BMRB 17916), quantifying agreement via RMSD and Pearson correlation of predicted versus experimental S² and Rex values. Statistical significance of improvement (p < 0.05) and a success threshold of >0.8 correlation enhancement relative to AlphaFold alone and homology-initiated MD will determine hypothesis validation.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly tests the causal role of AlphaFold structural basins in enabling accurate dynamic ensemble predictions by integrating rigorous enhanced sampling MD and validated NMR observables extraction, advancing beyond prior efforts that either focus solely on static predictions or lack systematic benchmarking against experimentally sensitive dynamic metrics. The combined use of enhanced sampling protocols and multi-faceted NMR validation represents a novel, mechanistically grounded framework for next-generation protein ensemble prediction.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating co-evolutionary constraints from deep metagenomic MSAs with scalable, physics-informed molecular simulation filtering enables accurate prediction of transient protein conformational ensembles that AlphaFold and similar methods currently fail to resolve.

BACKGROUND:  
While AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold predict high-accuracy static protein structures, they predominantly capture the most thermodynamically stable conformations and struggle to represent transient, functionally relevant states critical for dynamic protein function. Co-evolutionary signals embedded in extensive metagenomic sequence data encode residue-residue interactions reflective of alternative conformations, but lack explicit physical plausibility filtering, limiting their utility for transient state prediction. Bridging this gap is essential for modeling protein dynamics and conformational heterogeneity beyond static snapshots.

APPROACH:  
We propose a hybrid modeling framework that integrates co-evolutionary features extracted from large-scale metagenomic MSAs (MGnify dataset) with physics-based constraints derived from short, scalable molecular dynamics (MD) relaxations and force-field evaluations (e.g., AMBER or CHARMM energy functions) during structure prediction. This conformational selection mechanism selectively enriches biophysically plausible transient states encoded by evolutionary constraints by rejecting non-physical conformations, thereby enabling accurate reconstruction of conformational ensembles rather than single static models.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will compare (1) the hybrid model combining co-evolutionary inputs with physics-based simulation filtering against (2) an ablation model using identical co-evolutionary inputs but without physical constraints, and (3) leading baselines AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold. Evaluation will be performed on proteins from the Protein Ensemble Database (PED) exhibiting experimentally validated transient conformations, using ensemble RMSD improvements (targeting ≥1.0 Å over AlphaFold2) and Jensen-Shannon divergence of predicted versus experimental conformational population distributions. Statistical power and controls varying MSA depth and independent application of physical constraints will isolate causal contributions.

NOVELTY:  
This work concretely operationalizes the conformational selection principle by combining evolutionary and physics-based data at scale, overcoming co-evolutionary noise and stable-state bias that limit prior methods. Unlike earlier approaches that treat co-evolutionary and physical modeling independently or focus on static states, our integrated framework selectively filters and enriches transient conformations, providing a mechanistically grounded and scalable advance in dynamic protein structure prediction.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate enhanced sampling molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with AlphaFold static predictions to generate physically realistic conformational ensembles that improve the accurate recovery of functionally relevant protein states beyond AlphaFold alone.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold produces highly accurate static protein structure predictions but fails to capture the full dynamic ensemble of biologically relevant conformations critical for function, as described by the conformational selection model (Boehr et al., 2009). Existing methods lack rigorous integration of experimentally validated dynamic sampling, limiting their ability to predict alternative functional states. There is a need to causally test whether MD-derived physically grounded conformational ensembles can meaningfully enhance structure prediction in a functionally relevant manner.

APPROACH: Starting from AlphaFold-predicted structures, we will apply enhanced sampling MD techniques—such as metadynamics and Markov State Models (MSMs)—with well-validated force fields and solvent models to generate converged conformational ensembles. We will compare these against both AlphaFold static predictions and control ensembles generated by non-physical random perturbations and normal mode analysis to isolate the causal effect of physically realistic dynamics on functional state recovery.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate performance on proteins with experimentally characterized conformational heterogeneity from the Protein Ensemble Database (PED) and a curated subset of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) containing multiple ligand- or state-dependent structures. Using stringent RMSD thresholds and ensemble coverage metrics defined by alignment to experimental conformers, we will statistically test (>10% improvement, p < 0.05) whether MD-refined ensembles outperform AlphaFold alone and physically informed controls in recovering functionally relevant states.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously establishes the causal mechanism that physically realistic protein dynamics, as sampled by enhanced MD simulations, uniquely improve functionally relevant conformational predictions beyond AlphaFold’s static models. Unlike prior MD-augmented methods, it incorporates systematic convergence validation, standardized metrics, and physically meaningful controls to definitively demonstrate the added value of dynamic ensemble integration for protein structure prediction.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Explicitly modeling post-translational modifications (PTMs) within protein structure prediction frameworks—via incorporation of their chemical and physicochemical effects—will improve local conformational accuracy near PTM sites by capturing PTM-induced alterations in side-chain environments and local secondary structure, as demonstrated by comparisons against ablation baselines that ignore PTMs.

BACKGROUND: Current state-of-the-art protein structure predictors like AlphaFold2 rely primarily on unmodified amino acid sequences and thus fail to capture stable, PTM-induced local conformational rearrangements that arise from chemical alterations of side chains. Although AlphaFold and related models achieve near-experimental accuracy for global folds, they systematically miss PTM-specific local structural changes crucial for understanding PTM-driven functional regulation. Addressing this gap is critical for extending predictive accuracy to biologically relevant modified protein states.

APPROACH: We propose a PTM-augmented protein structure prediction model explicitly incorporating PTM chemical groups and their local physicochemical consequences—termed the PTM-Chemical Environment Modeling (PTM-CEM) mechanism—that alters side-chain electronic, steric, and hydrogen bonding constraints near modification sites. The model will be trained or fine-tuned on experimental structures annotated with PTMs, while a mechanism ablation baseline treats modified residues as unmodified to isolate the effect of explicit PTM modeling. This approach targets improved local conformational predictions without altering global fold predictions for PTMs primarily affecting dynamics.

EXPERIMENT: Using curated datasets combining PhosphoSitePlus and dbPTM annotations linked to high-resolution (<2.5 Å) experimental structures of phosphorylated, acetylated, and methylated proteins, we will benchmark (1) standard AlphaFold2 predictions on unmodified sequences, (2) the PTM-augmented model, and (3) the ablation baseline ignoring PTMs. Success metrics include local RMSD and side-chain rotamer recovery within 5 Å of PTM sites, targeting >20% improvement over ablation and AlphaFold2, with global GDT-TS differences constrained below 2%. Statistical significance across multiple PTM types and proteins will be assessed to falsify the PTM-CEM mechanism if no local improvements emerge.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that treats PTMs implicitly or ignores their chemical effects, this proposal explicitly models PTM-induced local chemical environment changes within structure prediction frameworks and rigorously tests their causal impact via mechanism ablation controls. By integrating high-confidence PTM annotations and matched PTM/unmodified experimental structures, it advances beyond sequence-driven predictors and static, unmodified models to capture stable PTM-specific conformational states critical for functional interpretation.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrating AlphaFold’s high-accuracy static protein structures with enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics simulations enables accurate prediction of intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) conformational ensembles, improving correlation with experimental NMR relaxation data beyond static prediction alone.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold2 excels at predicting static, folded protein structures representing local energy minima, it does not capture the dynamic conformational heterogeneity critical for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). IDP function depends on flexible ensembles poorly represented by single static models, and existing IDP modeling techniques often lack integration with high-confidence structural priors. Accurately predicting IDP ensembles remains an open challenge in structural biology.

APPROACH: We propose a causal mechanism termed AlphaFold-Initiated Dynamic Sampling (AIDS), wherein AlphaFold2 static models serve as meaningful starting points for enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—specifically replica exchange MD and metadynamics—to overcome energy landscape barriers and generate converged conformational ensembles of IDPs. By leveraging physics-based MD refinements initiated from AlphaFold predictions, we aim to capture both local structural preferences and global flexibility, producing ensembles that quantitatively reproduce NMR relaxation observables.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark on a curated set of IDPs with paired NMR relaxation datasets from DisProt (e.g., Sic1, α-synuclein, p53 transactivation domain). Two pipelines will be compared: (1) enhanced-sampling MD simulations initialized from AlphaFold2 predictions, and (2) direct use of AlphaFold2 static structures without MD refinement. Ensembles from both will be analyzed using a validated computational framework to predict NMR relaxation parameters (R1, R2, heteronuclear NOE) and order parameters (S²). Performance will be quantified by Pearson correlation coefficients and RMSD against experimental data, with statistical significance assessed by permutation testing (ΔR > 0.15, p < 0.05). Additional baselines include physics-only MD from extended conformations and established IDP ensemble methods like Flexible-Meccano and TraDES.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly formalizes and tests the causal mechanism that AlphaFold’s static models serve as superior initial conditions for enhanced-sampling MD to accurately model IDP ensembles, integrating deep learning and physics-based approaches with rigorous falsification using NMR data. Unlike prior studies that apply AlphaFold only for static prediction or focus on stability/complexes, this approach advances IDP modeling by overcoming sampling limitations and providing a quantitative ensemble-to-NMR mapping framework, establishing a new paradigm for protein dynamics-informed structure prediction beyond AlphaFold.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating persistent spectral graph features with deep neural network embeddings improves classification accuracy on high-dimensional biomedical datasets by capturing complementary topological and geometric information beyond what either modality achieves alone.

BACKGROUND:  
High-dimensional biomedical data such as single-cell RNA-seq profiles and brain connectomes exhibit complex intrinsic topological structures critical for accurate classification of cell types or cognitive states. Existing deep neural network (DNN) embeddings excel at extracting hierarchical nonlinear patterns but often overlook multi-scale topological and geometric connectivity information. Classical topological summaries, like persistent homology barcodes, are limited in capturing integrated spectral properties that reflect both shape and connectivity across scales.

APPROACH:  
We propose a causal mechanism termed **persistent spectral topology integration**, which combines persistent spectral graph features—derived from filtrations of combinatorial Laplacians on simplicial complexes—with learned DNN embeddings into a unified representation. This integration leverages the robust multi-scale topological invariants encoded by persistent spectral features alongside the rich nonlinear discriminative embeddings learned by deep models, yielding a complementary feature set optimized for classification tasks.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will conduct controlled comparative classification experiments on benchmark high-dimensional biomedical datasets—specifically, the PBMC 68k single-cell RNA-seq dataset (Zheng et al., 2017) and the Human Connectome Project (HCP) resting-state fMRI parcellations—with four model arms: (1) DNN embeddings alone, (2) persistent spectral graph features alone, (3) concatenation of DNN embeddings with classical persistent homology summaries, and (4) integrated persistent spectral graph + DNN embeddings. Classification accuracy on cell-type or cognitive state labels will be evaluated using stratified cross-validation, with a priori power analysis ensuring detection of ≥5% absolute accuracy gains at p < 0.01. Controls include permutation tests with randomized spectral features and mutual information analyses to confirm non-redundancy.

NOVELTY:  
This work distinguishes itself by explicitly leveraging persistent spectral graph theory—which fuses topological persistence with spectral geometric analysis—as a complementary representation to deep embeddings, rather than relying solely on classical homology or standard spectral graph neural networks. The approach is grounded in a rigorously falsifiable causal mechanism supported by theoretical representational analyses and robust empirical validation on topology-sensitive biomedical datasets.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Incorporating higher-order topological invariants such as persistent cohomology and zigzag persistence, which capture richer algebraic and temporal filtration structures beyond persistent homology, significantly improves clustering accuracy of high-dimensional biological single-cell datasets by encoding nuanced directional and dynamic connectivity patterns.

BACKGROUND: Standard topological data analysis (TDA) methods like persistent homology often fail to fully capture complex biological data’s intrinsic shape, especially when cell states exhibit continuous trajectories, branching, or temporal evolution. Existing approaches typically rely on homology-based summaries that ignore algebraic structures such as cup products or dynamic subspace changes, limiting their ability to discriminate biologically meaningful clusters in high-dimensional scRNA-seq data.

APPROACH: We leverage the causal mechanism that persistent cohomology and zigzag persistence provide functorially richer invariants sensitive to orientation, algebraic cup products, and filtrations indexed by dynamic or non-monotonic parameters, thus encoding temporal and directional features absent in persistent homology. We develop scalable pipelines for computing, vectorizing, and embedding these higher-order summaries on large-scale single-cell datasets, feeding them into clustering algorithms like spectral clustering and HDBSCAN to test whether they yield improved cluster separability over standard PH.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark on three complex high-dimensional biological datasets with known cell type labels: Paul et al. (2015) hematopoietic scRNA-seq, Kang et al. (2018) immune response scRNA-seq, and the Chua et al. (2020) SARS-CoV-2 single-cell atlas. Quantitative evaluation using adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI) will compare clustering using features from (1) persistent homology (PH) alone, (2) persistent cohomology (PC), and (3) zigzag persistence (ZP), against baselines including PCA/UMAP-reduced raw data and Mapper-based PH clustering. Statistical significance will be assessed through permutation tests, defining success as ≥10% improvement in ARI or NMI by PC or ZP over PH on at least two datasets.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior TDA applications that focus solely on persistent homology for static shape summaries or visualization, our work explicitly incorporates algebraically and filtrationally richer invariants—persistent cohomology’s cup product structure and zigzag persistence’s ability to track dynamic connectivity changes—combined with scalable, consistent vectorization pipelines and rigorous causal ablation, thereby providing a mechanistically grounded, quantitatively validated framework for enhanced topological clustering in biologically complex, high-dimensional data.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating joint spatial-temporal filtrations to compute multi-parameter persistent homology (MPPH) enables disentangling complex fault signatures in rotating machinery vibration data by capturing interactive spatial and temporal topological features that single-parameter filtrations overlook, thereby improving fault classification accuracy and robustness.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately detecting fault-related features in vibration data from rotating machinery is challenging due to the intertwined spatial correlations across sensor arrays and temporal evolution patterns of faults. Standard single-parameter persistent homology and classical feature extraction methods often analyze spatial or temporal dimensions independently, potentially missing the joint latent topological structures that characterize complex faults. This gap limits the discriminatory power of existing approaches in realistic, multi-sensor environments with artifact-controlled and balanced datasets.

APPROACH:  
We propose a multi-parameter persistence pipeline that constructs explicit joint spatial-temporal filtrations on multi-sensor vibration data, preserving the causal mechanism—called the Joint Spatial-Temporal Filtration Mechanism—whereby MPPH captures interactive fault signatures embedded simultaneously in spatial correlations and temporal dynamics. This approach is contrasted with ablated single-parameter filtrations restricted to either spatial-only or temporal-only axes, each followed by identical dimension reduction (e.g., UMAP or PCA) and rigorous stability analysis using quantitative measures such as persistence diagram bottleneck distances and feature persistence lifetimes. Baseline comparisons include standard single-parameter persistent homology pipelines and classical feature sets, such as Fourier spectral features and graph-based features derived from SuperGraph.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will validate the hypothesis on two benchmark datasets: the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) Bearing Data Center dataset, providing labeled, severity-graded faults under controlled conditions, and the Paderborn Bearing Dataset, offering spatially-distributed multi-sensor temporal sequences under realistic operational variability. Performance will be assessed via stratified cross-validation on balanced, artifact-controlled subsets, using fault classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score as primary metrics. The hypothesis is supported if the MPPH pipeline yields at least a 5% statistically significant (p < 0.05) improvement in F1-score over the best single-parameter persistent homology baseline, and if ablation by removing joint filtrations structurally degrades feature stability and classification results.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely formalizes and experimentally validates the Joint Spatial-Temporal Filtration Mechanism within multi-parameter persistent homology for machinery fault diagnosis, addressing theoretical challenges of stability and interpretability specific to joint filtrations. It advances beyond existing single-parameter TDA and classical methods by embedding a rigorously controlled ablation study and scalability considerations on complex multi-sensor datasets, thus providing the first practically feasible and theoretically justified demonstration that multi-parameter persistence reveals richer, interaction-driven topological fault signatures inaccessible to prior approaches.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Combining persistent spectral graph methods with neural network latent space embeddings enhances detection of robust, biologically meaningful multiscale topological features in high-dimensional biological data beyond what either approach achieves alone.

BACKGROUND: High-dimensional biological datasets, such as single-cell transcriptomics and protein conformational dynamics, exhibit complex geometric and topological structures that are challenging to characterize using conventional dimensionality reduction or topological data analysis (TDA) methods alone. Existing approaches either focus on purely topological persistence or nonlinear embeddings but fail to synergistically leverage multiscale geometric and hierarchical latent representations to uncover richer biological insights.

APPROACH: We propose the causal mechanism of *representational complementarity* whereby persistent spectral graph analysis applied to neural network-derived latent spaces (e.g., from variational autoencoders) systematically reveals stable topological features that are obscured in raw data or latent spaces alone. This method integrates multiscale spectral filtrations with nonlinear, hierarchy-disentangled embeddings to reshape data manifolds, enhancing topological persistence detection and biological interpretability.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate three conditions on the Human Cell Atlas scRNA-seq dataset and Protein Data Bank molecular dynamics trajectories: (1) persistent spectral graph applied to raw data, (2) persistent spectral graph on neural latent embeddings, and (3) baseline latent space TDA without spectral graph methods (e.g., Mapper and persistent homology). Metrics include the count and persistence lifetime of topological features surpassing rigorously defined noise thresholds, statistical significance via bootstrapped null models and randomized embedding controls (e.g., PCA, t-SNE), and biological relevance assessed through correlation with known cell types or protein states. Power analysis will guide sample sizes to ensure robust inference.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that treats spectral graph theory and latent embeddings independently or applies topological methods solely for visualization, our approach formally integrates persistent spectral graph theory with learned nonlinear latent spaces underpinned by topological stability theorems and representational complementarity principles. This fusion offers a novel mechanistic framework and scalable pipeline that jointly exploits geometric and hierarchical data representations to uncover non-redundant, interpretable topological signals in complex biological systems.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Applying multi-parameter persistent homology with carefully defined secondary filtrations to temporal high-dimensional datasets disentangles interacting parameter effects—this “Parameter-Interaction Disentanglement Mechanism” reveals richer, stable, and interpretable topological features that improve prediction of system state transitions beyond single-parameter persistence.

BACKGROUND: Classical persistent homology relies on single-parameter filtrations, typically monotonic in time, which conflates multiple interacting dynamics into ambiguous topological signatures, limiting insight into complex, non-monotonic, and multi-scale system behaviors. Current topological and dimensionality-reduction methods often fail to capture joint parameter evolution or provide stable, interpretable invariants suitable for forecasting critical transitions in high-dimensional temporal data, such as mechanical degradation or patient clinical states.

APPROACH: We operationalize the secondary filtration parameter as a discretized measurement scale or physiological variable aggregation level, rigorously justified via preliminary stability and independence analyses to ensure complementary topological information beyond time. Multi-parameter persistence invariants—such as rank invariants and Hilbert functions—are computed using scalable approximation algorithms benchmarked on representative datasets, controlling feature dimensionality and model complexity. These topological summaries feed into predictive models (random forests and temporal convolutional networks) to forecast imminent system state transitions, isolating the “Parameter-Interaction Disentanglement Mechanism” by ablating multi-parameter features in favor of single-parameter time filtrations as a baseline.

EXPERIMENT: Using the NASA C-MAPSS Turbofan Engine Degradation and PhysioNet Challenge 2012 ICU patient datasets, we evaluate predictive performance via AUC and PR-AUC for critical state transitions within fixed horizons, comparing multi-parameter persistence, single-parameter persistence, UMAP, Mapper graphs, and standard statistical feature baselines. Statistical significance is assessed with paired bootstrap tests, requiring >5% absolute predictive gains with p < 0.01 to support the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work introduces a principled framework for defining and justifying multi-parameter filtrations tailored to temporal high-dimensional data, incorporates scalable computational methods with rigorous complexity controls, and explicitly formalizes and tests the “Parameter-Interaction Disentanglement Mechanism”—a causal explanation for improved predictive power beyond prior multi-parameter persistence applications focused primarily on visualization or static datasets.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models trained on integrated multi-omic single-cell datasets from phylogenetically related vertebrates learn transferable representations of conserved regulatory grammar that improve prediction of functional regulatory elements in under-studied species, outperforming RNA-only and single-omic baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Cross-species identification of conserved regulatory elements remains challenging due to noisy and species-specific gene expression profiles. Chromatin accessibility data provide orthogonal signals that mark functional regulatory elements with higher evolutionary stability, but existing models rarely integrate multi-omic single-cell data across species to leverage this regulatory conservation. This gap limits transfer learning effectiveness for under-annotated organisms despite available reference genomes.

APPROACH:  
We propose training large transformer-based foundation models (e.g., multi-omic adaptations of SCALEX or scBERT) on integrated single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from mouse, rat, and human to learn joint embeddings reflecting conserved regulatory grammar—defined here as the disentangling of transcriptional noise from regulatory element activity via multi-omic integration. A critical ablation trains the same architecture on RNA-only data to isolate the causal mechanism of chromatin accessibility integration. Rigorous controls including species label permutation and domain adversarial training will be applied to mitigate confounders related to batch effects and evolutionary divergence.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be evaluated on enhancer prediction in the naked mole-rat using independent orthogonal epigenomic assays—bulk ATAC-seq peaks and histone modification ChIP-seq from ENCODE/NHP epigenomic projects—and fine-tuned with available single-cell RNA-seq and/or multi-omic data from this species when possible. Performance metrics will include PR-AUC and ROC-AUC, with >10% PR-AUC improvement of multi-omic models over RNA-only models as strong evidence supporting the hypothesized mechanism.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior foundation models and cross-species predictors by explicitly leveraging multi-omic single-cell data integration across multiple vertebrates to learn conserved regulatory grammar, validated through targeted mechanism ablation and rigorous confounder controls, providing a novel framework for transferable regulatory element prediction in under-studied species.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Transfer learning from foundation models pretrained on large-scale human single-cell RNA-seq data, combined with rigorous species-specific orthology mapping and domain adaptation techniques to explicitly mitigate interspecies distributional shifts, improves annotation of conserved cell states in closely related non-human primates with limited single-cell data.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately annotating cell states in non-human species with scarce single-cell datasets remains a key challenge due to species-specific transcriptomic divergence and limited labeled data. Existing cross-species integration methods often fail to leverage large human single-cell resources fully or to systematically disentangle conserved biological signals from species-specific noise. There is a pressing need for principled transfer learning approaches that incorporate evolutionary conservation and address distributional mismatch to enable robust cell state annotation across species boundaries.

APPROACH:  
We propose a biologically grounded causal mechanism—termed the “Conserved Regulatory Transfer Mechanism”—which posits that shared gene regulatory programs and transcriptional signatures underpin conserved cell states across closely related species. To operationalize this, we first apply comprehensive orthology mapping (using Ensembl Compara and OrthoDB) with explicit handling of ambiguous, many-to-many, or missing orthologs, including careful treatment of functionally analogous non-orthologous genes. During fine-tuning of human-pretrained foundation models on non-human primate datasets (e.g., Macaque Brain Atlas, Chimpanzee Cell Atlas), we apply domain adaptation algorithms such as adversarial domain adaptation and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) minimization to align feature distributions and reduce species-specific biases. Ablation studies will separately remove orthology mapping and domain adaptation to isolate their individual contributions, including negative controls transferring to distantly related species and random gene mappings to test transfer limits.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate annotation performance on held-out labeled subsets of non-human primate single-cell RNA-seq data, benchmarking F1 score and adjusted Rand index against expert manual labels. Baselines include (1) models trained solely on limited non-human data, (2) transfer learning without orthology mapping or domain adaptation (the ablation), and (3) traditional label transfer methods such as Seurat’s CCA and joint embedding. Statistical significance of improvements (targeting >10% relative F1 gain with p < 0.05 by bootstrapping) will confirm the mechanism. Additional validation includes cross-dataset generalization, uncertainty quantification, and biological plausibility assessment of predicted annotations.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates large-scale foundation models with a rigorously defined evolutionary conservation framework and domain adaptation tailored to single-cell transcriptomics, going beyond prior cross-species integration approaches that lack explicit orthology-based feature alignment and distributional shift mitigation. Our detailed ablation and negative control experiments provide the first causal test of the “Conserved Regulatory Transfer Mechanism,” clarifying the necessary conditions for effective cross-species transfer learning in single-cell biology.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pre-trained on integrated multi-omics single-cell data (joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq) can more accurately predict cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks than identical models pre-trained solely on bulk transcriptomic data, due to their ability to capture cell-type-resolved regulatory heterogeneity.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate inference of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) is critical for understanding cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms in complex tissues. Bulk transcriptomic datasets obscure cellular heterogeneity by averaging signals across diverse cell types, limiting the resolution and accuracy of GRN predictions. Although foundation models (FMs) have shown promise in representing biological data, it remains unresolved whether multi-omics single-cell pre-training confers a causal advantage in recovering true cell-type-specific regulatory interactions.

APPROACH:  
We will develop two foundation models with identical architectures: one pre-trained on large-scale multi-omics single-cell datasets (e.g., the 10x Genomics Multiome PBMC dataset from the Human Cell Atlas) integrating scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq modalities using robust data harmonization techniques to mitigate modality heterogeneity, scale imbalances, and noise; and a second pre-trained solely on matched bulk RNA-seq data from GTEx tissues. Additionally, an ablation model pre-trained on single-modality single-cell data (scRNA-seq alone) will isolate the contribution of multi-omic integration. Downstream, all models will be fine-tuned to predict cell-type-specific GRNs.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark predicted GRNs against experimentally validated, cell-type-resolved TF-target interactions curated from ENCODE and DoRothEA databases in immune cell subtypes, quantifying performance via F1 score and area under precision-recall curve (AUPR).
