Unlike prior scaling laws focused on dataset size or compute, it explicitly models and tests how domain diversity interacts with model capacity via a formal capacity-limited generalization mechanism, supported by a novel domain coherence ablation that causally disentangles domain structure from token-level statistics.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Controlled defect engineering induces a stable partial coupling between threshold switching (TS) and memory switching (MS) states in memristor devices—termed Defect-Engineered TS-MS Coupling—which enables adaptive energy scaling by dynamically entering low-power threshold states during inactivity without losing stored synaptic information, achieving significant power reduction with negligible accuracy loss in neuromorphic computing.

BACKGROUND:  
Neuromorphic computing demands ultra-low power operation, particularly during the prevalent low-activity periods characteristic of spiking neural network (SNN) workloads. Existing memristive synapses exhibit either stable memory switching or threshold switching behaviors but lack adaptive energy scaling capabilities because TS and MS states are uncoupled, preventing low-power standby modes without data loss. Addressing this gap requires engineering memristor devices at the defect level to create a controllable energetic landscape that enables dynamic, non-volatile low-power states aligned with workload activity.

APPROACH:  
We propose fabricating two cohorts of HfO₂-based memristor arrays: one with precise defect engineering to create Defect-Engineered TS-MS Coupling, and an ablation baseline without such engineering yielding decoupled TS and MS behaviors. This coupling harnesses defect states as tunable energy barriers modulating ion/vacancy migration dynamics, enabling stable, adaptive transitions between memory and threshold states. Both device sets will be embedded in neuromorphic crossbar arrays running SNN inference on the Dynap-se dynamic visual pattern recognition and N-MNIST datasets, allowing statistical characterization of low activity epochs and enabling evaluation of adaptive power scaling under real-world temporal sparsity.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will measure continuous energy consumption and inference accuracy during SNN operation, focusing on power savings during statistically defined low activity periods. Metrics include achieving ≥15% average power reduction relative to the ablation baseline and maintaining <1% accuracy degradation. Rigorous endurance and retention tests under dynamic workloads will validate stability, while system-level controls ensure isolation of the defect-induced coupling effect from software or peripheral management.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior reports of coexistence of TS and MS by explicitly engineering defect states to achieve a stable, partial TS-MS coupling that enables dynamic, non-volatile low-power threshold states for adaptive energy scaling—demonstrated through direct mechanistic validation and controlled ablation baselines—thus providing the first experimentally validated pathway for memristive devices to reduce power consumption adaptively in neuromorphic workloads without sacrificing computational fidelity.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) with memristive synapses enables at least 30% reduction in neuromorphic circuit energy consumption by leveraging low-voltage, non-volatile ferroelectric switching, without compromising synaptic plasticity fidelity.

BACKGROUND: Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in scaling neuromorphic computing hardware, where synaptic weight storage and modulation dominate power consumption. Conventional memristive synapses suffer from relatively high switching energies and leakage currents, limiting their utility for large-scale, low-power neural networks. Addressing these limitations by exploiting novel device physics could enable more practical, energy-efficient neuromorphic architectures.

APPROACH: We propose a hybrid synaptic device that integrates FTJs with memristors to harness the ferroelectric polarization switching mechanism, which offers low coercive fields and tunnel electroresistance effects for energy-efficient, precise analog conductance tuning. This hybrid design reduces programming energy and leakage while maintaining stable, linear, and symmetric weight updates critical for synaptic plasticity, thereby enabling energy-efficient on-chip learning.

EXPERIMENT: We will fabricate and benchmark three matched synaptic arrays—memristor-only, FTJ-only, and FTJ-memristor hybrid—employing identical network architectures trained on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. Energy profiling will be conducted with time- and cycle-resolved in situ measurements separating switching, leakage, and peripheral overheads, while synaptic plasticity fidelity will be assessed via weight update linearity, symmetry, retention, and final classification accuracy. Success requires ≥30% energy reduction in the hybrid array versus memristor-only, with <2% accuracy degradation; falsification occurs if these criteria fail or if the memristor-only baseline matches hybrid energy efficiency, negating the ferroelectric causal mechanism.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior memristor-based neuromorphic devices, this work explicitly isolates and quantifies the energy savings attributable to ferroelectric tunnel junction integration through rigorous ablation controls and detailed energy decomposition. By combining theoretical device physics modeling with comprehensive experimental validation, it advances beyond incremental improvements to demonstrate a scalable, manufacturable pathway for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing not yet addressed in the literature.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating dynamically reconfigurable 2D ferroelectric synaptic devices with neuromorphic architectures will reduce synaptic energy consumption by over 30% compared to state-of-the-art HfO₂-based memristors, driven by lower-voltage ferroelectric polarization switching.

BACKGROUND: Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in neuromorphic computing hardware, where synaptic devices often consume excessive power due to high-voltage, ion-migration-based switching in memristors. While 2D ferroelectric materials offer promising non-volatile polarization states for synaptic weight modulation, challenges in scalable integration, device reliability, and clear mechanistic understanding have limited their practical application and rigorous comparison to memristors.

APPROACH: We propose fabricating neuromorphic circuits on silicon platforms implementing identical spiking neural network topologies with synapses based on 2D ferroelectric materials (e.g., α-In₂Se₃ or CuInP₂S₆) and HfO₂ memristors as baselines, alongside an ablation baseline where ferroelectricity in 2D devices is suppressed via controlled thermal annealing or doping. This approach leverages Landau-Khalatnikov-governed ferroelectric switching to achieve lower energy synaptic updates by reducing switching voltage and current leakage, supported by quantitative modeling of switching energetics and endurance.

EXPERIMENT: We will measure energy per synaptic update during training and inference on publicly available neuromorphic datasets—specifically N-MNIST for spiking neural networks and DVS Gesture for dynamic vision sensor processing—using calibrated on-chip voltage and current monitoring under matched operation frequency and device area. Success requires statistically significant >30% energy reduction in 2D ferroelectric synapses versus memristors, with the ablation baseline performing comparably to memristors to confirm the causal role of ferroelectric switching.

NOVELTY: This work provides the first rigorous, mechanism-driven comparison of 2D ferroelectric synapses against industry-relevant HfO₂ memristors with a robust ferroelectric suppression ablation control, integrating detailed theoretical modeling and scalable fabrication strategies to address reliability and variability, thereby advancing beyond prior memristor- or 2D-material-centric neuromorphic demonstrations toward practical, energy-efficient synaptic devices.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Employing **Metaplasticity-Gated Long-Term Potentiation (MG-LTP)**—a synaptic plasticity mechanism that selectively permits LTP only during periods of elevated but submaximal network activity—can reduce synaptic energy expenditure by over 30% while preserving effective long-term learning in neuromorphic spiking neural networks.

BACKGROUND:  
Current neuromorphic computing systems face energy inefficiencies due to indiscriminate synaptic potentiation during all levels of network activity, including noise-driven or low-salience inputs. This leads to redundant synaptic updates that waste metabolic and computational energy, undermining the energy efficiency benefits of neuromorphic architectures. Existing plasticity models often lack adaptive gating mechanisms informed by synaptic metaplasticity, which naturally regulates learning thresholds to prevent runaway potentiation and optimize energy use.

APPROACH:  
We propose MG-LTP, a dynamic metaplasticity mechanism that modulates the LTP induction threshold based on recent network activity statistics, effectively gating LTP to epochs of elevated yet non-maximal firing rates indicative of salient inputs. This gating leverages established synaptic tagging and capture theory and homeostatic metaplasticity principles to reduce unnecessary potentiation events while maintaining memory consolidation. The mechanism will be implemented on scalable neuromorphic SNN simulators with fine-grained synaptic energy profiling, enabling direct measurement of synaptic update energy costs coupled with matched activity controls to isolate true energy savings.

EXPERIMENT:  
The MG-LTP model will be benchmarked against two baselines—(1) standard STDP with fixed LTP thresholds (no gating), and (2) a memristor-modeled synapse with linear, non-metaplastic weight updates—using the N-MNIST and DVS Gesture neuromorphic datasets. Metrics include total synaptic energy expenditure (via weighted synaptic update counts validated against hardware profiling), classification accuracy (target within 2% of baseline), and synaptic update distribution analysis to confirm selective potentiation. Ablation of MG-LTP gating will serve as a falsification test: failure to reduce energy by >30% or to preserve accuracy within 2% will reject the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focusing on memristive device physics or static plasticity models, this study explicitly integrates synaptic metaplasticity to dynamically gate LTP based on network-level activity patterns, targeting energy savings by preventing potentiation during low-salience activity. It uniquely combines rigorous theoretical modeling, hardware-validated energy profiling, and scalable neuromorphic benchmarks to causally link adaptive gating with significant synaptic energy reduction without compromising learning performance.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Neuromorphic synaptic devices integrating layered perovskite materials as active elements will demonstrate at least 30% lower energy consumption per synaptic event compared to state-of-the-art all-2D van der Waals synapses, owing to intrinsically reduced ion migration barriers and tunable ferroelectric polarization dynamics.

BACKGROUND:  
Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing demands synaptic devices that minimize energy per synaptic event while maintaining reliable plasticity. Although all-2D van der Waals synapses offer excellent weight update linearity and stability, their energy consumption remains limited by intrinsic material switching properties. Layered perovskites, with their lower ionic migration activation energies and stable ferroelectric phases, present a promising avenue to fundamentally reduce switching energy, yet this potential has not been rigorously isolated or experimentally verified against 2D vdW baselines.

APPROACH:  
We will fabricate matched neuromorphic synapses using layered perovskite materials and benchmark them directly against all-2D van der Waals synapses under identical device geometries and operating protocols derived from the 2021 “A Reliable All-2D Materials Artificial Synapse” framework. The causal mechanism—defined as the coupled ionic migration-ferroelectric polarization switching dynamic predicted by Arrhenius ion diffusion models and Landau-Ginzburg-Devonshire ferroelectric theory—will be tested via mechanism ablation controls using independently validated ion migration suppression methods (chemical passivation, low-temperature operation, and novel barrier-engineering techniques) to decouple ionic and ferroelectric contributions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Device performance will be evaluated on the public Neuromorphic Image Signal Processing Dataset (NISP) with standardized pulse schemes; key metrics include average energy consumption per synaptic event measured by high-precision electrical instrumentation, weight update linearity and symmetry, and cyclability over ≥10,000 events. Statistical significance will be established from large samples (n≥20 per device type) across repeated training runs, with falsification criteria defined as less than 10% energy reduction or failure of energy increase under ion migration suppression exceeding 15%.

NOVELTY:  
This study is the first to rigorously isolate and quantify the fundamental material physics—specifically ion migration and ferroelectric switching kinetics—in layered perovskites as the dominant mechanism for energy savings in neuromorphic synapses, using mechanism ablation controls and matched 2D vdW device baselines. This multiscale experimental-theoretical integration surpasses prior memristor and 2D synapse work by providing definitive causal evidence linking layered perovskite intrinsic properties to neuromorphic energy efficiency gains.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators for cryosphere model acceleration that incorporate *Temporal Attention Mechanisms for Nonlinear Feedback Disentanglement*—selectively weighting past states across timescales guided by physically informed features and regularization—can more accurately and robustly capture nonlinear feedbacks in cryosphere dynamics than fixed-window recurrent or feedforward baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Representing nonlinear feedback loops in cryosphere dynamics, such as permafrost thaw and albedo changes, remains a key challenge due to their complex temporal dependencies occurring over slow to abrupt timescales. Existing emulators often rely on fixed-window recurrent architectures or feedforward networks that inadequately model these temporal complexities, limiting their predictive fidelity and robustness under abrupt transition scenarios, which hinders climate model acceleration and policy-relevant simulations.

APPROACH:  
We propose a deep learning emulator architecture employing temporal attention mechanisms that dynamically focus on relevant historical states and inputs over varying timescales, explicitly disentangling nonlinear cryosphere feedbacks. This attention is informed and constrained by physically meaningful input features and regularization to prioritize domain-relevant signals and mitigate overfitting. We conduct comprehensive ablation studies comparing the full temporal attention model against (1) a fixed-window recurrent model (LSTM/GRU) and (2) a feedforward baseline without temporal modeling, isolating the contribution of selective temporal weighting.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be trained and evaluated on multi-region cryosphere time series datasets, including the Permafrost Carbon Network and ESA CCI Cryosphere satellite-derived products, augmented with rigorously validated synthetic abrupt thaw scenarios generated via process-based perturbations of thermal and moisture variables. Success metrics include RMSE and MAE for soil temperature, active layer thickness, and surface albedo; correlation of predicted versus observed nonlinear feedback indices (e.g., rates of active layer deepening); and robustness quantified as relative performance degradation under synthetic abrupt thaw perturbations. The hypothesis is supported if the temporal attention model achieves statistically significant (>10%) improvements in error metrics, feedback correlation >0.7 (vs. <0.5 for ablations), and less than 15% performance degradation under perturbations.

NOVELTY:  
This work introduces the *Temporal Attention Mechanism for Nonlinear Feedback Disentanglement* in cryosphere emulation, going beyond prior deep learning emulators that use fixed-window recurrent or static architectures by explicitly modeling selective temporal dependencies critical to cryosphere feedbacks. It uniquely combines physically informed inputs, validated synthetic scenario augmentation, and rigorous multi-variant ablations to robustly link architecture design to improved nonlinear feedback representation and climate model acceleration.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Incorporate soft physical conservation constraints alongside stochastic parameterizations in deep learning emulators to synergistically stabilize multi-year climate variable predictions by guiding outputs toward physically plausible states while capturing unresolved process variability.

BACKGROUND: Climate model emulators enable faster simulations but often suffer from long-term instability and drift, particularly in conserved quantities like energy and moisture. Purely stochastic emulators can capture variability but may fail to maintain physical realism over extended rollouts, while deterministic models without constraints risk unphysical divergence, limiting their applicability for climate projections.

APPROACH: We propose a hybrid emulator architecture that enforces approximate physical conservation laws as soft constraints or regularization terms during training, combined with stochastic parameterizations to represent subgrid and chaotic processes. This “Soft-Constrained Stochastic Stabilization” mechanism directs the emulator toward physically consistent states without reducing its nonlinear expressivity, while stochasticity prevents collapse onto overly smooth or biased trajectories, jointly improving long-term stability and accuracy.

EXPERIMENT: Using CESM Large Ensemble (CESM-LE) multi-year climate state outputs, we will train four emulator variants: (1) deterministic baseline without constraints or stochasticity; (2) deterministic with soft conservation constraints only; (3) stochastic only (e.g., stochastic ConvDeepONet); and (4) combined soft constraints plus stochasticity. We will evaluate multi-year (5-year) rollout performance using normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) on conserved variables and a rigorously defined drift metric measuring cumulative deviation in total energy and moisture budgets relative to ground truth, with ablations varying constraint strength to isolate causal effects.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior physics-informed or stochastic emulators that apply either hard constraints or stochasticity independently, our method introduces a theoretically grounded synergy by softly regularizing conservation laws as differentiable penalties integrated with stochastic parameterizations, supported by constrained optimization and stochastic dynamical systems theory. This approach explicitly tests and quantifies the unique load-bearing role of soft constraints in stabilizing long-term climate emulation beyond stochasticity alone, a gap not addressed by existing work.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators that explicitly embed physical conservation laws within their architectures will achieve more stable and physically consistent long-term climate model acceleration than purely data-driven emulators, without sacrificing short-term accuracy.

BACKGROUND:  
Current deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration often suffer from error accumulation and physical inconsistency over long simulation horizons, limiting their utility for decadal climate projections. While physics-informed machine learning has shown promise in enforcing physical constraints, a rigorous, systematic comparison quantifying the causal impact of embedded conservation laws on emulator stability and fidelity in complex coupled climate systems remains lacking.

APPROACH:  
We propose training two classes of deep learning emulators on CESM Large Ensemble outputs: (1) physically-constrained models integrating mass, momentum, and energy conservation explicitly via architecture design (e.g., physics-informed neural networks or equivariant networks) and (2) purely data-driven models using standard architectures such as convolutional LSTMs or transformers without physical constraints. To ensure stable long-term recursive prediction, we incorporate curriculum learning, teacher forcing, and error correction techniques, while precisely defining conservation violation metrics at emulator resolution with strict numerical tolerance thresholds.

EXPERIMENT:  
Emulators will be evaluated on multi-step prediction tasks spanning from 1 month to 10 years by recursively feeding predictions as inputs, using RMSE against CESM ground truth and conservation violation metrics (e.g., net flux divergence) as primary benchmarks. Baselines include the original CESM subgrid parameterizations and hybrid models with physics constraints as penalty terms. The hypothesis will be falsified if purely data-driven emulators match or exceed the long-term fidelity and physical consistency of physically-constrained models.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances prior physics-informed ML by rigorously isolating the causal effect of explicit conservation law embedding on long-term climate emulator stability through comprehensive ablation controls and physically interpretable metrics, addressing trade-offs between model expressivity and physical realism in complex climate dynamics over decadal timescales.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Physically constrained deep learning emulators that enforce hard conservation law constraints via projection-based architectures will achieve at least 20% lower out-of-sample prediction error on subgrid-scale climate processes than unconstrained or softly constrained deep neural networks.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately representing subgrid-scale (SGS) turbulence and mixing processes in climate models remains a crucial bottleneck limiting predictive fidelity and computational efficiency. Existing deep neural network emulators often ignore explicit physical laws, risking physically inconsistent outputs and poor generalization to unseen climate states. Embedding strict physical constraints as inductive biases may reduce the hypothesis space to physically plausible solutions, improving predictive accuracy and robustness in climate model acceleration.

APPROACH:  
We propose deep learning emulators employing physics-informed neural network (PINN) architectures with hard constraints explicitly enforced via constrained optimization and projection layers that guarantee exact conservation of mass, momentum, and energy throughout training and inference. This contrasts with soft constraint variants that penalize constraint violations in the loss but do not guarantee strict physical consistency. By limiting the model’s hypothesis space to physically admissible states, our approach seeks to improve generalization on out-of-sample SGS climate data.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be trained and evaluated on high-resolution subgrid turbulence data from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB) for stratified shear flows, supplemented with CESM2 outputs featuring explicit SGS parameterizations. We compare: (1) the hard-constrained PINN emulator, (2) an identical unconstrained deep neural network baseline (Ling et al., 2020 architecture), and (3) a soft-constrained ablation variant. Performance is measured by relative reduction in root mean squared error (RMSE) for SGS viscosity and diffusivity predictions on a held-out spatiotemporal test set, with a required improvement threshold of ≥20% RMSE decrease over the unconstrained baseline, coupled with physical consistency scores and statistical significance testing to confirm robustness.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously distinguishes and implements true hard physical constraint enforcement mechanisms—beyond conventional physics-informed losses—to guarantee exact conservation laws in deep learning climate emulators, addressing a gap in prior SGS emulation literature. It provides a formal causal test of inductive bias from hard constraints on generalization, with comprehensive experimental controls isolating constraint effects from architectural or optimization confounds.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained on harmonized multi-model climate simulation ensembles exhibit improved distributional robustness and generalization to unseen extreme warming scenarios compared to emulators trained on single-model outputs, by capturing broader climate system variability and structural uncertainties.

BACKGROUND:  
Current deep learning emulators of climate subgrid-scale processes often rely on single Earth System Model (ESM) outputs, limiting their ability to generalize to out-of-distribution climate regimes such as extreme warming scenarios. This constrains the utility of emulators in accelerating climate projections under unprecedented forcing conditions, where physical responses and feedbacks may differ substantially from historical or moderate scenarios. Overcoming this challenge requires leveraging model diversity to enhance emulator robustness without incurring overfitting or bias.

APPROACH:  
We propose training deep neural network emulators on carefully curated and harmonized subgrid-scale process outputs (e.g., turbulent fluxes, radiative transfer variables) from multiple CMIP6 ESMs (CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, UKESM1.0), capturing inter-model variability and parameterization differences to increase distributional coverage. A matched emulator is trained solely on CESM2 data with identical architecture and training procedures, enabling a controlled causal test of the “multi-model diversity” mechanism for improving distributional robustness. Additionally, a baseline with randomized ensemble labels removes model identity while preserving data volume, disentangling the effects of diversity versus data quantity.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate emulator predictive skill on CESM2 “ssp585-future extreme” scenario outputs, which feature forcing levels and feedbacks outside training distributions. Metrics include root mean square error (RMSE) and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) relative to ground truth CESM2 simulations, with success defined as at least 15% RMSE reduction and improved CRPS for the multi-model emulator over the single-model emulator. Additional out-of-distribution tests include perturbed physics ensembles and independent extreme scenario outputs from other CMIP6 models to verify generalization and control for temporal autocorrelation and data imbalance.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly quantifies how multi-model ensemble diversity enhances emulator distributional robustness using formal metrics of inter-model variability and domain generalization theory, a step beyond prior single-model deep emulators or classical statistical approaches. We introduce rigorous data harmonization and mechanism ablation controls—randomized label baselines and balanced training data—to isolate the causal impact of multi-model training diversity on extreme climate extrapolation skill, addressing key practical barriers to deploying deep emulators in climate acceleration workflows.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating curated biosynthetic pathway data from Nigerian indigenous medicinal plants into transformer-based generative models will induce a pathway-informed inductive bias that improves the target specificity and selectivity of novel drug candidates beyond models trained solely on global drug-like molecular databases.

BACKGROUND:  
Current generative AI models for drug discovery predominantly rely on large global molecular databases like ChEMBL, which often lack rich biosynthetic context from region-specific natural products. This limitation restricts the models’ ability to generalize to biologically optimized chemical scaffolds evolved in indigenous medicinal plants, particularly those relevant to endemic diseases such as malaria. Leveraging pathway-level biochemical knowledge from these plants could fill an important gap, enabling generation of compounds with higher functional specificity and translational relevance.

APPROACH:  
We will develop two matched transformer-based generative models (Chemformer variants): (1) a Pathway-Enriched Model trained on a combined dataset of ChEMBL 31 plus curated biosynthetic pathway data from Nigerian indigenous medicinal plants (sourced from NPASS and ethnobotanical literature), and (2) a Global-Only Model trained exclusively on ChEMBL 31. The key mechanism, termed “Pathway-Inductive Bias,” posits that embedding biosynthetic transformations and scaffold motifs from indigenous pathways constrains generation to biologically meaningful chemical space, enhancing target binding specificity. Both models will be trained with identical parameters and dataset sizes to isolate this causal effect.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will generate libraries from both models targeting validated Plasmodium falciparum enzymes implicated in malaria. Computational evaluation will include docking affinity via AutoDock Vina, selectivity indices computed from MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations against target/off-target homologues, and chemical novelty/synthetic accessibility scoring. Top candidates unique to each model (n=20 per group, selected via predefined synthetic feasibility filters) will be synthesized and subjected to in vitro binding assays with surface plasmon resonance using validated protein constructs. Statistical significance of improved affinity/selectivity in the Pathway-Enriched Model outputs will be assessed by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p < 0.01). Negative controls will include models trained on size-matched chemically diverse non-pathway datasets to rule out confounding effects.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly operationalizes indigenous medicinal plant biosynthetic pathways as a novel domain-specific inductive bias within transformer generative models, advancing beyond existing natural product–informed approaches by integrating pathway mechanistic knowledge rather than isolated compound data. It critically tests the evolutionary optimization hypothesis for plant metabolites in human disease contexts via rigorous in silico and in vitro validation, establishing a mechanistic link between biochemical pathway data inclusion and improved out-of-distribution generalization and target specificity, a connection not previously demonstrated at this scale or granularity.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporate differentiable proxy metrics of synthetic accessibility as a multi-objective conditioning signal during training of diffusion-based generative models to explicitly bias latent space toward synthetically feasible chemical regions, thereby increasing the proportion of generated molecules predicted by retrosynthesis tools to be synthesizable within three steps.

BACKGROUND: Generative AI models for drug discovery often produce molecules that are novel yet impractical to synthesize, limiting their translational impact. Existing methods either ignore synthetic accessibility (SA) during training or apply post-hoc filtering, missing opportunities to embed synthesizability as an inductive bias that guides molecular generation. A key challenge is disentangling synthetic feasibility from other correlated molecular properties to produce diverse, novel, and realistically synthesizable compounds.

APPROACH: We propose to integrate differentiable synthetic accessibility proxies—such as continuous RAscore or differentiable retrosynthesis likelihood estimates—directly into the conditioning vector of diffusion-based molecular generative models, enforcing a multi-objective optimization that balances SA with drug-likeness features. This “SA-Inductive Bias” mechanism explicitly shapes the latent space toward synthetically feasible chemotypes during training. We will compare this to an ablation baseline trained identically but without SA conditioning, isolating the causal impact of SA signals on latent space structure and output synthesizability.

EXPERIMENT: Using the MOSES benchmark dataset, we will train two diffusion models (with and without SA conditioning) and generate a large, fixed number of molecules (e.g., 50,000 each). We will evaluate (1) the fraction of molecules with ≤3-step retrosynthetic routes predicted by ASKCOS and IBM RXN (using repeated runs and consensus scoring to manage retrosynthesis variability), (2) internal scaffold diversity via Tanimoto similarity of Morgan fingerprints, and (3) novelty relative to the training dataset. Latent space interpolation and clustering analyses with quantitative metrics will assess embedding disentanglement and the SA mechanism’s load-bearing role. Negative controls will include random conditioning baselines and post-generation filtering comparisons to ensure causal attribution.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies SA heuristics as post-processing filters or uses non-differentiable proxies, our approach leverages differentiable SA metrics as an explicit multi-objective conditioning signal during diffusion model training, directly guiding latent representations toward synthesizability. This enables mechanistic insights through latent space analysis and rigorously quantifies trade-offs between synthetic accessibility, diversity, and novelty—advancing beyond existing generative frameworks lacking integrated SA inductive bias.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporating active learning with standardized human-in-the-loop (HITL) expert feedback into generative AI molecular design models will causally improve the bioactivity of designed molecules by iteratively focusing exploration on chemically relevant regions, outperforming static training and random retraining baselines.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI approaches for drug discovery often rely on static datasets or unsupervised iterative retraining, which can limit exploration to known chemical space and yield suboptimal bioactivity. There is a critical need to systematically integrate human expertise to guide model refinement and prioritize biologically meaningful candidate molecules, thereby enhancing the efficiency and quality of de novo molecular design.

APPROACH: We propose a rigorously defined active learning framework with standardized human expert annotation protocols—including objective criteria for novelty, synthetic feasibility, and assay artifact control—that iteratively retrains a Transformer-based VAE generative model targeting SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). Human experts curate uncertain and promising molecules selected via uncertainty sampling to guide the next design batch, closing the experimental feedback loop; parallel control arms include static training, random iterative retraining without HITL, and uncertainty-only sampling without human feedback to isolate the impact of human guidance.

EXPERIMENT: Using a combined ChEMBL25 filtered dataset for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors and curated COVID Moonshot bioassay data, the experiment will synthesize and assay five sequential batches of 50 molecules per arm, retraining models after each iteration. Success metrics are mean and median in vitro IC50 values with a >30% reduction in mean IC50 for the HITL arm compared to static baseline, assessed via Mann-Whitney U test (p < 0.05), with falsification defined by lack of HITL improvement or ablation baseline parity.

NOVELTY: This study explicitly quantifies and standardizes human expert feedback within active learning for molecular design—differentiating it from prior work that either lacks iterative human curation or uses unsupervised retraining—and uniquely combines rigorous multi-arm controls, objective annotation protocols, and experimental validation to causally attribute enhanced bioactivity to human-in-the-loop guidance.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporating explicit 3D protein-ligand interaction constraints into diffusion-based generative models causally improves the generation of candidate molecules with significantly higher binding affinity than models trained solely on 2D molecular representations.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI models for drug discovery often rely on 2D molecular graphs or implicit 3D information, limiting their ability to accurately capture the spatial and physicochemical complementarity essential for high-affinity protein-ligand binding. This gap hampers the generation of molecules with optimal binding conformations, a critical factor in structure-based drug design. Addressing this challenge requires integrating explicit 3D protein-ligand interaction constraints to better represent the energetic and geometric determinants of binding affinity.

APPROACH: We propose a diffusion-based molecular generative framework explicitly conditioned on 3D protein-ligand interaction maps derived from experimentally resolved complexes, encoding spatial distances, interaction types, and physicochemical complementarity within binding pockets. This is contrasted with a baseline diffusion model trained solely on 2D molecular graphs without protein context. Both models will be carefully matched in architecture capacity and training protocols to isolate the causal effect of 3D interaction constraints on molecule quality.

EXPERIMENT: We will train and evaluate the models on the PDBBind v2020 refined set, using docking scores (AutoDock Vina, GNINA), rigorous free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations, and selected biophysical binding assays to quantify binding affinity improvements. Generalization will be assessed on the CASF-2016 benchmark. Success is defined by at least a 10% statistically significant increase (p < 0.01) in mean binding affinity and enrichment of strong binders (< -9 kcal/mol) for the 3D-constrained model relative to the 2D baseline, with ablation experiments removing 3D inputs to confirm causal impact.

NOVELTY: Unlike existing 3D-aware generative models that often embed implicit or global 3D features without explicit protein-ligand interaction conditioning, our method uniquely integrates detailed spatial and physicochemical interaction constraints from experimentally resolved complexes into a diffusion generative process. Furthermore, we rigorously combine computational and experimental validation with strict controls on model capacity and training, establishing a clear causal link between 3D interaction encoding and improved binding affinity in de novo molecular generation.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Integrate multi-modal generative AI models that explicitly incorporate curated, high-confidence static protein 3D structures combined with dynamic simulation-informed features to model protein binding site flexibility, thereby improving de novo drug candidate binding affinity and selectivity beyond ligand-centric or static-protein molecular models.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI approaches for drug discovery predominantly rely on ligand-only representations or static protein structures, failing to adequately capture protein conformational dynamics critical for molecular recognition. Ignoring protein flexibility and induced fit mechanisms leads to suboptimal ligand designs with higher false positive rates and reduced predictive accuracy of binding affinity and selectivity.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-modal generative framework that integrates three complementary input modalities: (1) molecular graphs representing ligand structures, (2) static high-confidence protein 3D structures from experimentally solved PDB entries or AlphaFold predictions, and (3) dynamic simulation-derived features such as RMSF-based residue flexibility maps, pocket volume fluctuations, and conformational cluster indicators obtained from enhanced sampling molecular dynamics trajectories. This integration explicitly encodes the causal mechanism—here termed the **Dynamic Binding Site Context Mechanism**—which captures spatial and energetic complementarity by modeling protein flexibility and ligand-induced fit effects. Ablation models omitting dynamic features or using ligand-only inputs isolate the contribution of dynamic context.

EXPERIMENT: Train three generative models on well-characterized targets including SARS-CoV-2 main protease (PDB 6Y2E) with MD datasets from D.E. Shaw and Folding@home, and human Abl kinase with public MD ensembles. Evaluate generated molecules using docking (Glide XP, AutoDock Vina), molecular dynamics-based binding free energy scoring (MM/GBSA, alchemical free energy perturbation where feasible), chemical novelty (QED), synthetic accessibility, and retrospective enrichment benchmarks on held-out actives and decoys. Statistical comparison will test whether the full multi-modal model yields ≥0.5 kcal/mol improved predicted binding free energies and ≥10% higher true positive enrichment versus ablation and ligand-only baselines. Experimental biophysical validation (e.g., SPR or ITC) on ~5 top candidates will corroborate computational predictions. Failure to observe statistically significant gains falsifies the Dynamic Binding Site Context Mechanism.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior generative AI drug design studies that rely on static protein structures or ensemble docking, this work is the first to explicitly encode and integrate dynamic simulation-derived binding site features as structured inputs within a generative model, enabling direct learning of protein flexibility effects on ligand optimization. The formulation and rigorous testing of the Dynamic Binding Site Context Mechanism distinguishes this approach by causally linking protein dynamics to improved ligand generation, with intermediate ablations and expanded computational and experimental validation ensuring mechanistic interpretability and robustness.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating domain-specific physical invariance constraints explicitly derived from known physical laws into causal discovery algorithms improves the structural identifiability and accuracy of causal graphs inferred from high-dimensional nonlinear time series beyond purely data-driven methods.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from observational nonlinear time series remains challenging due to high dimensionality, nonlinear interactions, hidden confounders, and limited sample sizes, often resulting in spurious or incomplete causal graphs. Existing methods rely predominantly on statistical dependencies and invariant causal prediction across environments but typically do not integrate mechanistic physical constraints known a priori from domain knowledge. Leveraging these physical invariance constraints can theoretically reduce the hypothesis space and improve causal identifiability, but systematic incorporation and validation remain underdeveloped.

APPROACH: We propose a causal discovery framework that formally encodes physical invariance constraints—such as conservation laws, symmetries, and known functional interaction forms—from domain knowledge as mandatory structural restrictions within the causal graph search or constraint satisfaction process. The method integrates these constraints alongside conditional independence testing and invariant causal prediction principles, explicitly handling noise and partial observability via robust optimization and latent variable modeling. This framework includes theoretical identifiability analysis demonstrating improved recovery guarantees when physical invariances hold.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate performance on three benchmark datasets with well-characterized physical laws and ground-truth causal structures or validated approximations: (1) Lorenz-96 model (nonlinear chaotic climate dynamics with energy conservation), (2) DREAM3 Systems Biology Challenge (gene regulatory networks with biochemical constraints), and (3) Physionet MIMIC-III clinical time series (with homeostatic physiological constraints). The physics-constrained causal discovery method is compared against its own ablation without physical constraints, and three state-of-the-art baselines—PCMCI+, TCDF, and Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP)—using Structural Hamming Distance (SHD, requiring ≥15% improvement), edge Precision and Recall, and temporal robustness of inferred causal relations across environment shifts. The hypothesis is falsified if the physics-informed method does not yield statistically significant improvements or reduces robustness and accuracy.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that treats domain knowledge as optional priors or focuses solely on statistical invariances, this approach formalizes the mandatory integration of explicit physical laws as invariance constraints into causal discovery, accompanied by theoretical identifiability guarantees. It rigorously evaluates the benefits and limitations of physical constraints across diverse complex nonlinear systems, providing a principled framework bridging mechanistic domain knowledge and data-driven causal inference beyond existing nonlinear time series methods.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Pretraining attention-based neural networks on synthetic causal graphs that explicitly incorporate latent confounding, feedback loops, and nonstationarity—the *Structural Inductive Bias Pretraining Mechanism*—enables the model to learn representations that disentangle true causal dependencies from spurious correlations in nonlinear dynamic systems, thereby improving robustness and sample efficiency in downstream causal discovery from real observational time series.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from nonlinear, high-dimensional time series with limited samples is fundamentally challenging due to latent confounders, feedback loops, and nonstationary dynamics that induce spurious correlations. Existing attention-based models typically train from scratch on limited real data, risking overfitting and poor generalization. There is a critical need for approaches that instill structural inductive biases reflecting real-world causal complexities, to enable more accurate and sample-efficient causal graph recovery.

APPROACH:  
We propose self-supervised pretraining of an attention-based neural network on a rigorously validated synthetic dataset of causal graphs that embed core real-world complexities: latent confounding, feedback loops, and nonstationarity. This *Structural Inductive Bias Pretraining Mechanism* guides the network to learn causal disentanglement representations beyond generic feature extraction. Experimental controls include pretraining on simplified synthetic graphs lacking these complexities, pretraining on unrelated synthetic data (e.g., independent noise processes), and training from scratch to isolate the effect of structural realism in pretraining.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate downstream causal discovery on benchmark real-world nonlinear time series datasets with known or well-validated ground truth causal graphs: the *CauseMe* Reservoir challenge dataset, the *Sachs* proteomic signaling dataset, and the *Climate* time series dataset. Metrics are average Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) for edge detection and Structural Hamming Distance (SHD). Statistical power analyses will determine dataset sizes and replicates, with a priori criteria that at least 10% improvement in AUPRC and 20% reduction in SHD over both simplified pretraining and no pretraining baselines support the hypothesis. Ablation of the pretraining mechanism complexity tests its necessity.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely formalizes and rigorously tests the *Structural Inductive Bias Pretraining Mechanism* by leveraging carefully validated synthetic causal graphs with realistic dynamic complexities, differentiating it from prior methods that either use generic or oversimplified pretraining or rely solely on conditional independence tests and handcrafted heuristics. Our approach explicitly bridges the gap between synthetic pretraining and real-world nonlinear causal discovery, providing theoretical and empirical insights into inductive bias benefits in dynamic causal inference.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating domain-specific causal constraints as explicit search space priors into nonlinear time series causal discovery algorithms reduces false positive causal edges and improves precision and F1-score without loss of recall in high-dimensional settings.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from observational high-dimensional nonlinear time series remains challenging due to the combinatorial explosion of candidate causal edges, leading to many false positives and overfitting to noise. While constraint-based frameworks assert that encoding expert knowledge can regularize causal graph search, there is a lack of rigorous empirical validation and theoretical clarity about the benefits and limitations of such constraints in nonlinear, temporally dependent data. This gap complicates reliable causal inference in domains like neuroscience and climate science where prior knowledge exists but may be incomplete or uncertain.

APPROACH: We propose to integrate domain-specific causal constraints—such as disallowed edges based on anatomical or physical impossibilities and enforced temporal directionality—directly as hard priors in state-of-the-art nonlinear causal discovery algorithms (e.g., PCMCI+, TCDF). These constraints act as a search space regularizing mechanism, theoretically reducing spurious conditional independencies and false positives by pruning implausible causal hypotheses. We will additionally quantify the impact of constraint quality by comparing correct, partial, incorrect, and random constraint sets to isolate the true causal mechanism.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate the constrained versus unconstrained algorithms on the CauseMe Challenge synthetic nonlinear time series datasets with known ground-truth graphs, measuring precision, recall, and F1-score, and require a statistically significant (p < 0.05, paired t-test) improvement of at least 15% in precision and F1 without loss of recall. For real-data validation, we will apply the methods to Human Connectome Project fMRI datasets, using expert-defined anatomical and physiological connectivity constraints and assessing reductions in false positive edges via consensus with neuroscientific knowledge and predictive accuracy of held-out interventional effects. Control experiments will test the effects of incorrect or random constraints to falsify the causal regularization mechanism if no improvement is observed.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior nonlinear time series causal discovery work that focuses primarily on algorithmic advances and conditional independence testing, this study rigorously formalizes and quantifies the role of domain-specific causal constraints as a search space regularizer in complex temporal data. It explicitly addresses challenges of constraint imperfection, nonstationarity, and high dimensionality, and introduces systematic falsification controls to disentangle the benefits of expert knowledge from generic model complexity reduction.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Integrating rigorously formalized domain-specific causal constraints as inductive biases into deep learning-based causal discovery frameworks improves the accuracy of causal direction identification in nonlinear time series beyond purely data-driven approaches.

BACKGROUND: Accurate causal discovery from nonlinear, high-dimensional time series is notoriously difficult due to spurious correlations and limited samples. Existing deep learning methods like TCDF achieve strong function approximation but often lack mechanisms to incorporate prior domain knowledge, limiting their ability to reliably infer causal directions, especially when temporal or structural constraints are known but underutilized.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting the Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) by encoding domain-specific causal constraints—such as temporal precedence and known non-causal relations—as explicit soft or hard regularizers within the attention mechanism and graph search, thus embedding inductive biases grounded in causal invariance. This constraint encoding is formalized via a computationally tractable mapping from qualitative domain knowledge to precise temporal and structural regularization terms, with mechanisms to handle uncertainty and fuzziness in expert knowledge.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate TCDF+Constraints against TCDF-Base, PCMCI+, and Runge et al.’s nonlinear causal discovery method on both synthetic datasets with known ground-truth causal graphs and real-world nonlinear time series datasets from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) program and PhysioNet Challenge 2012, using metrics including direction accuracy (>10% improvement expected), F1-score for graph recovery, and false positive rates of constraint-violating edges. A falsification ablation involves random permutation of constraints to control for generic regularization effects, with statistical significance assessed via repeated cross-validation and permutation testing.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that relies solely on data-driven discovery or generic regularization, this study rigorously formalizes and integrates domain-specific causal constraints as inductive biases within a deep learning causal discovery architecture, providing a reproducible framework to leverage known temporal and structural causal knowledge and systematically validating their impact on nonlinear time series causal inference accuracy.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating domain-specific causal constraints encoded as differentiable logic modules into deep causal discovery frameworks induces a constrained optimization mechanism that significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of causal direction identification in high-dimensional nonlinear time series compared to purely data-driven models.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational time series data remains challenging due to high dimensionality, nonlinear interactions, noise, and limited samples, which often lead to spurious correlations and ambiguous causal directions. Existing deep learning-based causal discovery frameworks, such as TCDF, rely solely on statistical patterns without systematically leveraging domain knowledge, limiting their identifiability and interpretability. There is a critical need for methods that incorporate domain-specific causal invariances and constraints in a mathematically principled, differentiable manner to guide causal inference in complex dynamical systems.

APPROACH:  
We propose embedding domain-specific causal constraints—such as temporal ordering, monotonicity, and known conditional independencies—as differentiable logic modules within a deep causal discovery architecture (e.g., TCDF). These modules translate causal rules into continuous, differentiable penalty terms or regularizers that restrict the causal graph search space during end-to-end training, embodying a causal invariance and constrained optimization mechanism. This approach integrates prior knowledge seamlessly with data-driven learning, providing inductive biases that improve identifiability and robustness without altering model architecture or hyperparameters.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct controlled experiments comparing the proposed constrained model against an ablation baseline without embedded constraints and a control condition with irrelevant/distractor logic modules, using three benchmark datasets with ground-truth causal graphs: (1) synthetic nonlinear Lorenz-96 chaotic systems, (2) fMRI time series from the Human Connectome Project with brain region causal priors, and (3) DREAM4 gene expression time series. Evaluation metrics include Structural Hamming Distance (target ≥15% reduction), and edge-level precision, recall, and F1-score (target ≥0.1 improvement) with non-overlapping confidence intervals across repeated trials to ensure statistical significance.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that either relies purely on data-driven deep causal discovery or non-differentiable incorporation of domain knowledge, our method uniquely formulates domain causal constraints as differentiable logic modules, enabling seamless and stable integration into end-to-end causal discovery optimization. This explicit embedding of causal invariances as continuous constraints is novel in high-dimensional nonlinear time series and is rigorously validated with controlled ablations and real-world datasets, extending beyond existing frameworks like TCDF or PCMCI+ that lack such principled inductive bias mechanisms.
